title: Guidance Before Autonomy
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article pushes back on the popular assumption that autonomy alone drives motivation, arguing that empowerment without adequate upfront guidance sets people up to flounder. The author lays out five things a leader should clarify before handing off a project: success criteria, constraints and guardrails, likely pitfalls, the leader's own hard-won experience (offered without obligation to follow it), and how often the leader wants updates. The piece treats these five clarifications as the scaffolding that makes real autonomy possible rather than reckless. It closes with the memorable framing that empowerment starts with direction, not the absence of it.
points: Empowerment without upfront guidance often robs team members of the direction they need to succeed, even though autonomy is broadly motivating.

Before delegating, leaders should clarify five things: criteria for success, constraints/guardrails, likely pitfalls, the leader's own experience-based advice (offered without obligation), and preferred update cadence.
Sharing past experience is valuable only if the leader explicitly frees the team from having to follow it exactly — otherwise guidance becomes disguised control.
Empowerment isn't abandonment; leaders still expect periodic updates so they can intervene if needed, without micromanaging.
quotes: But it is also common for empowering leaders to rob people of the guidance they need to do their best work. Even empowerment requires a confident and organized liftoff.
A discussion about the “criteria of success” paints a picture of what must happen for the project or task to be considered successful.
Think of this part of the discussion as clarifying the guardrails for the project. What boundaries exist, and how should the project adhere to them?
Describing what they have seen work in the past can be a tremendous asset to the team, as long as they are free to reject some or all of the advice.
Before people can climb, they must first embrace the ladder. The leader brings the scaffold.
